summary: Defines the Static Context Header Compression and fragmentation framework, designed for Low-Power Wide Area Networks. Compression relies on a static context kept both on the device and in the network, and the document gives a generic mechanism and its use for IPv6 and UDP headers, plus optional fragmentation.

plainLanguage.summary: SCHC reduces repeated header information by letting both ends use the same preconfigured Rules. It can also split a packet into fragments when the link cannot carry it at once.

questions: how does schc compress ipv6 and udp headers
what are the schc fragmentation modes
subtitle: Static rules compress headers and optionally split packets for constrained networks.

tldr.problem: Low-Power Wide Area Networks carry small payloads, while IPv6 and UDP headers and IPv6's MTU requirement can exceed what a link can carry.
tldr.mechanism: Both ends share static Rules. The sender replaces known header values with a RuleID and sends only the remaining bits; optional modes fragment larger packets.
tldr.outcome: The generic framework compresses IPv6 and UDP headers and defines optional fragmentation. Technology-specific settings belong in Profiles. RFC 9441 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 8724 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2020. It has been updated by RFC 9441; technology-specific settings are defined in Profiles.

sections.title: Constraints in Low-Power Networks
sections.content:
Low-Power Wide Area Network (LPWAN) devices may sleep for long periods and send very small data units. A return path may be costly, restricted, or unavailable, so header compression that needs frequent synchronization is a poor fit.

Static Context Header Compression and fragmentation (SCHC) uses shared Rules known in advance. The framework also defines optional fragmentation to help an LPWAN support IPv6's 1280-byte MTU requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices have little power and can send only small amounts of data. SCHC uses settings already known at both ends, so they do not need to exchange updates for every packet.

sections.title: The SCHC Packet and Shared Context
sections.content:
SCHC sits between an upper-layer protocol such as IPv6 and an underlying LPWAN. Compression runs first. If the compressed result is still too large for the link, a Profile may direct the system to fragment it.

A SCHC Packet contains a compressed header followed by the original payload. The compressed header contains a RuleID and any Compression Residue. Both endpoints must have the same Rules and Profile before communication begins; the generic RFC leaves their provisioning and technology-specific settings to other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends keep the same set of Rules. The sender identifies a matching Rule and sends its identifier with only the header bits that still need to be carried.

sections.title: Rules and Field Descriptors
sections.content:
A Rule contains Field Descriptors in header order. Each descriptor names the field, its length and position, the packet direction, a target value, a matching operator, and a compression/decompression action.

The compressor finds a Rule matching all and only the packet's header fields. It can omit a known value, send a value or a mapping index, send only changing low bits, or let the decompressor compute a field. If no Rule matches, the packet header is sent uncompressed under a designated RuleID.
sections.plainLanguage: A Rule says which header fields to check and what to send for each one. If both ends already know a value, the sender can leave it out and the receiver restores it.

sections.title: Matching and Rebuilding Header Fields
sections.content:
The matching operators are equal, ignore, MSB(x), and match-mapping. They test whether a packet field matches a fixed value, accept any value, compare leading bits, or find a value in a list.

Actions determine how the receiver rebuilds a field. For example, not-sent uses the Rule's target value, LSB combines known leading bits with transmitted low bits, and compute-* recomputes a value after its inputs are rebuilt.
sections.plainLanguage: The Rules can compare a field with a known value or list. They also tell the receiver whether to restore, combine, or calculate the field.

sections.title: Fragmentation Messages and Integrity
sections.content:
Fragmentation divides a SCHC Packet into non-empty, non-overlapping tiles. Depending on the mode, tiles may be grouped into windows and acknowledged with a bitmap. Messages include SCHC Fragment, SCHC ACK, SCHC ACK REQ, Sender-Abort, and Receiver-Abort.

The All-1 Fragment marks the last tile; with windows, All-0 marks the end of a non-final window. The receiver checks packet integrity after reassembly. The RFC recommends a CRC32 RCS using polynomial 0xEDB88320.
sections.plainLanguage: When needed, SCHC sends a packet as numbered pieces. The receiver rebuilds it and checks the result before accepting the packet.

sections.title: Three Fragmentation Modes
sections.content:
No-ACK sends fragments without feedback and assumes packets arrive in order; it can work on a one-way link. ACK-Always waits for an acknowledgment after each window and retransmits missing tiles before continuing.

ACK-on-Error supports variable link MTU and out-of-order delivery. It sends acknowledgments for windows with missing tiles, so the sender may move ahead while earlier windows remain unconfirmed. Profiles specify which modes and parameter values a technology uses.
sections.plainLanguage: No-ACK sends pieces without waiting for replies. The two acknowledgment modes use a return path to report missing pieces, either after each group or when an error occurs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A packet with an unknown RuleID should be silently dropped. The decompressor should not rebuild a packet larger than the Profile's MAX_PACKET_SIZE; the generic default is 1500 bytes. Rules can also be written so secret fields do not change the compressed message length.

Fragmentation can expose devices to buffer-reservation and forged-ACK attacks. The RFC also discusses privacy of DTag values and the possibility of using fragmentation to bypass network inspection.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can use fragments to consume receiver resources, so devices need limits and integrity checks. Compression Rules also need care when packet length could reveal a secret.
